Overview: Meal Memory takes a new approach nutrition tracking, helping diabetes understand how their meals affect their blood sugar. It is the first mobile application released by the company I founded Databetes.

My Role: UI/UX, Data Visualization, Visual Design, Strategy

Design/Process: For diabetes patients, managing their meals is one of the biggest challenges. Yet interviews with dozens of patients revealed that the vast majority do not log any of their meals or related medical data. Existing solutions make self-tracking a cumbersome and time consuming process. Patients also complain that the feedback that they get on all the data they just logged is lacking. As a result, patients will try an app for a few days, then stop using it.

Meal Memory is designed to be both a sustainable solution and one that provides actionable insights. Logging a meal is faster and easier because it starts with taking a photo instead of entering text. A patient can also enter a pre-meal blood sugar reading, a carbohydrate estimate and notes.

Two hours later, we send an alert to the phone asking for a post-meal blood sugar. With these two data points from before and after eating, patients can see whether they've balanced their food and medication correctly. This information can then be retrieved when they eat this meal again, allowing them to make a better informed decision about their medication dosage.

To simplify the presentation of data, blood sugar readings are sorted as low, in range or high. Each of these three categories are color-coded. The pre-meal blood sugar appears as a dot on the left, the post-meal on the right. A photo feed displays the patient's meal history with these before and after data points presented on top. Clicking on a photo gives more detailed information on that meal.

Together, Meal Memory more closely resembles a consumer photo service rather than a traditional health app. It makes meal logging something more rewarding and feel less like a chore, encouraging patients to make it a frequent habit.

I'm not a Linux expert but I wanted to share a few things about what works best for me on a System76 Lemur with an i3 for gaming on Ubuntu. This is a lightweight mobile laptop and not a powerhouse. But with a few tweaks I can play games like Counter Strike: Global Operations and Talos Principle just fine. On my first run, I was getting like 15 fps in CSGO and I knew I could do better.

After some research, I put the following in the terminal:

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:xorg-edgers/ppa
sudo apt-get update

That installed better drivers for me. Apparently this can fuck up your PC in some cases. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Another neato trick is

sudo apt-get install linux-tools-common
sudo apt-get update

Now, I can use

cpupower frequency-set -g performance

Which I've monitored to bring my CPU frequency up from 1.1 GHz to the full 2+GHz I purchased.

Connect to a powersource! I'm not sure if this is a BIOS thing, but this adds a few more frames-per-second to your games. Be careful not to let your computer get too hot. Additional cooling is a smart decision.
